legs.scotts-peak>junction-creek: Register at the booth at Huon Campground, scrub boots at the wash-down station, then follow the Port Davey Track south (some maps label it McKays Track). Myrtle-sassafras forest gives way within about a kilometre to buttongrass and heath; early boardwalk ends and the pad becomes rutted, knee-deep mud in places. Walk through the mud rather than widening the braids. Several unbridged creek crossings can rise fast and become impassable in heavy rain; if in doubt wait it out or turn back. Plenty of water from creeks and pools along the way.
legs.junction-creek>moraine-a-foot: Cross Junction Creek and continue south on the Port Davey Track; the first fork is McKays Track heading east across the Arthur Plains (your A–K return route), so keep right on the Port Davey Track. The track here is muddy and badly braided, with some newer boardwalk. At the second junction the Port Davey Track carries on south-west towards Port Davey while the signed Western Arthurs track turns up towards Alpha Moraine. Fill every bottle at the stream with a small sandy beach at the moraine foot: it is the last reliable water until the Lake Cygnus area.
legs.moraine-a-foot>moraine-a-top: The big climb of the trip: roughly 800 m of ascent in about 3 km up Alpha (A) Moraine, steepest at the bottom and again near the top, on eroded steps, white quartzite gravel and deep ruts. Few flat rest spots; pace it with a full pack and plenty of water. Views open back over Lake Pedder, Scotts Peak and Mt Anne. The crest is very exposed to westerly fronts; a tiny emergency tent spot sits behind rocks and bushes near the top. In poor weather this is the place to decide whether to go on or drop back to Junction Creek.
legs.moraine-a-top>capella-crags: Head south-east across an exposed moor on stepping stones and rock-paved track below the western face of Mt Hesperus (summit side trip possible). The route then boulder-hops and scrambles beneath Hesperus to the saddle between Hesperus and the Capella Crags, which overlooks Lake Fortuna (side trip from the saddle). Only small moorland pools for water. In cloud, follow the rock work and cairns carefully; the moor is featureless in whiteout.
legs.capella-crags>lake-cygnus: Scramble through the Capella Crags on a well-worn line, then descend steeply to Lake Cygnus on constructed rock stairs and tight switchbacks. At the junction on the descent turn right (signed) to reach the camp; the main range route continues from this junction tomorrow, so you will climb back up the same way. Combined with the moraine climb this makes a long, demanding first range day; allow 4–6 h for Junction Creek to Cygnus (PWS).
legs.lake-cygnus>mt-hayes: Climb back up to the junction above the lake (a solid start to the day with cold legs), then head south-east along the rocky, very exposed crest on well-made rock paving below a line of spires. The track contours below the Mt Hayes summit; the summit itself is a short unmarked side trip (about 40 min return). Fill up at Cygnus, as the next reliable water is the stream before Square Lake.
legs.mt-hayes>procyon-peak: Drop steeply off the southern shoulder of Mt Hayes into a shaded chute, pass beneath a slanting rock spire and descend loose, unstable rock on the eastern side to a saddle. Climb a smaller summit south of Procyon Peak on uneven track, then traverse the western face of Procyon; the route skirts the 1136 m summit. Expect hands-on scrambling in and out of rocky gullies (PWS); take care with loose rock above other walkers.
legs.procyon-peak>square-lake: Descend gently off Procyon towards Square Lake. A boggy crossing leads into a small patch of forest with a stream: the most dependable water of the Cygnus–Oberon day, so top up here. Square Lake has big boulders by the shore for a break or swim, and informal sites at and above the lake if weather forces an early stop.
legs.square-lake>orion-saddle: A strenuous, rooty and rocky climb leads out of the Square Lake basin to the saddle between Mt Orion and Mt Sirius, where Lake Oberon comes into view for the first time. Both peaks are short unmarked side trips from here (leave packs at the saddle). Phone reception is sometimes available on Sirius and nearby high points. The Epsilon Moraine, a little north-west of Orion, is the emergency escape to the Arthur Plains from this part of the range.
legs.orion-saddle>lake-oberon: At the junction just below the Orion saddle take the right-hand track down to Lake Oberon. The descent runs under a huge grey cliff down a rutted chute of broken boulders with exposed scrambling; some parties lower packs, others downclimb wearing them. Lower down, pandani and scoparia scrub give way to boardwalk and stepping stones to the lake. PWS describes this section as steep and very rough; it is a good test of whether the party is ready for what follows.
legs.lake-oberon>mt-pegasus: From here the range becomes markedly harder and more dangerous (PWS): fair weather and an early start only, as parties queue at the hauls. Carry a full day of water from Oberon, enough to reach High Moor or even Haven Lake. Climb south-east past a small tarn to a saddle overlooking Lake Oberon and the Arthur Plains, then follow cairns up a boulder wall where packs may need to be passed up. At the base of a sheer cliff follow the cairns right around it rather than trying to climb it, and retrace if you meet a vertical drop. Just below the summit you squeeze through a hole or cave among precarious boulders; pack hauling is essentially required (a second tunnel can be bypassed on the right).
legs.mt-pegasus>mt-capricorn: About 100 m past the summit the route drops down a steep gully and traverses beneath a buttress, where boulders have large gaps over deep drops (PWS). Descend the eastern face on white quartzite through dense scrub; misleading pads branch off, so follow cairns. A balcony high above Lake Uranus, some pinnacles and another steep drop lead to the saddle below Mt Capricorn, then a scramble over grey boulders to the top. Marked only by intermittent cairns; navigation is hard in cloud.
legs.mt-capricorn>high-moor: Capricorn's descent is very steep, down eroded earth steps and a fern-and-scrub-covered slope where you hang onto branches; take it slowly when wet. A small bivvy cave on the descent fits about three in an emergency. From the flat saddle, pools near Dorado Peak may hold water in a wet season. Finish with a climb past Mt Columba and boardwalks onto High Moor.
legs.high-moor>beggary-bumps: Carry all of today's water (4–5 h of hard going at least): there is no reliable source until Haven Lake. Climb onto the Beggary Bumps, then plunge down a shaded chute where tea-tree and pandani serve as handholds. The route then traverses the southern slopes high above Lake Ganymede, using horizontal tree trunks for support. PWS rates the Bumps plus Tilted Chasm as the hardest part of the traverse.
legs.beggary-bumps>mt-taurus: The crux is Tilted Chasm, a steep descent between two tilted slabs that is often damp and mossy; it looks so improbable that people doubt they are on route. Many parties haul or lower packs at the top and bottom; others climb down wearing them using the coarse holds. Next comes The Dragon: a muddy pad, then an enjoyable scramble near its top, turning east before the peak and dropping off the southern shoulder through gnarled trees and boulders. Continue over exposed boulders past Lovers Leap and the Little Beggaries; one awkward boulder drop before Taurus uses tree limbs for support. Fine-weather tent spots are in the saddle before Mt Taurus, about 15–20 min short of Haven Lake.
legs.mt-taurus>haven-lake: The Mt Taurus summit is an optional short scramble. From the eastern shoulder a flat boulder gives your first view of Haven Lake, then a tricky boulder descent and a scrubby slope lead to the lake. PWS allows 4–6 h for the whole High Moor to Haven stage, but slow parties or a hauling queue at Tilted Chasm can easily push it longer.
legs.haven-lake>lake-sirona: Climb out of the Haven cirque on steps and grippy rock to the saddle above the lake (the Mt Aldebaran side trip starts near here). A technical ridge follows, traversing around rocky tors on the steep side, then a descent over loose shale into a sloping meadow and on to a boulder peak above Lake Sirona. The final drop to the lake is steep, eroded and exposed over broken boulders; the last move is a squeeze between two boulders onto a sloping slab, easier with packs off. About 1 km, typically 30–60 min.
legs.lake-sirona>mt-scorpio: Refill at Lake Sirona: on the A–K it is the last reliable water until Seven Mile Creek on the plains, and on the full traverse until Lake Vesta. Cross the south-east shore and climb gently through open moorland on rocked track to Mt Scorpio, with one brief exposed slab near the end. The walking is far easier than anything since Oberon, but still fully exposed to westerly weather. Scorpio is the last reliable spot for mobile coverage.
legs.mt-scorpio>kappa-moraine-top: Descend the escarpment east of Mt Scorpio for about half an hour to the top of Kappa (K) Moraine. Here the route forks: north-east down Kappa Moraine for the A–K exit, or south towards Lake Vesta for the full traverse. Make the commit-or-exit call here; beyond this point the full traverse is more overgrown and much less travelled.
legs.kappa-moraine-top>seven-mile-creek: A long, knee-jarring descent of about 700 m. The upper moraine is steep and rough though not technical, with views of Lakes Vesta and Juno and Promontory Lake. Lower down the gradient eases, and near the base a junction leads out onto the Arthur Plains, often muddy. Rusted stakes mark the line across buttongrass to the scrub along Seven Mile Creek, which is easy to lose in overgrown sections or at dusk. An unmarked shortcut runs more directly towards Two Mile and Junction Creek and saves about 4 km. It is not on maps and parties regularly lose it, so use it only with good navigation and a GPS.
legs.seven-mile-creek>wullyawa-creek: Cross Seven Mile Creek (usually shallow, wet feet likely) and follow orange arrows away from the creek onto McKays Track. A long north-west traverse over open buttongrass plains follows, with boggy patches and occasional dips into scrubby creek gullies; gaiters and long pants help. Wullyawa Creek is hidden in a shaded scrub band and crossed on logs. After heavy rain, plains creeks can be hard to cross, so allow time to wait. About 2 h.
legs.wullyawa-creek>two-mile-creek: A short stretch through a strip of mossy forest, then back onto open plains on slightly higher, gravelly ground. Muddy hollows and small creeks punctuate the walking. Around 45 min.
legs.two-mile-creek>junction-creek-r: Continue west on McKays Track for about 45 min to its junction with the Port Davey Track and turn right (north). Drop down to Junction Creek and cross it to the camp; the PWS notes that drier sites are south of the creek, so pick one before you cross if it is in flood. PWS gives 18.5 km and 7–10 h for the full Haven Lake to Junction Creek day.
legs.junction-creek-r>scotts-peak-r: Retrace the first day north along the Port Davey Track: muddy at first, then boardwalked sections and a final stretch of tall forest to the boot-wash station and Huon Campground (PWS 8.4 km, 3–4 h). Creek crossings may be higher than on the way in after rain. Sign out at the registration booth so your trip is closed off.
legs.kappa-moraine-top>lake-vesta: Take the south fork at the top of Kappa Moraine. The pad heads north at first and then swings south into a narrow, steep gully following a stream valley down to Lake Vesta. From here on the track is fainter and scrubbier, with scratchy vegetation, so long sleeves and pants are worth wearing. Lake Vesta has a few sheltered sites on its north-east side; trailhiking lists them as emergency-use only for A–K walkers.
legs.lake-vesta>lake-juno: A short but steep descent from Lake Vesta to Lake Juno. There is a small campsite near the Juno outlet (halfwayanywhere) that is useful if weather closes in. Water is plentiful at both lakes.
legs.lake-juno>promontory-lake: Climb roughly 100 m from Lake Juno up to Promontory Lake. Follow the northern and eastern shores, which is further than it looks, to the campsites in the south-east corner. The site is poorly sheltered and squally afternoon winds are common, so pitch low and guy out well. Haven Lake to Promontory is about 5 km and around 5 h (trailhiking).
legs.promontory-lake>the-phoenix: Fill all bottles before leaving: sources mention no reliable water between Promontory Lake and Lake Rosanne, a long day. Head south-east on a faint pad through thinning scrub, past the knoll called The Sculpture, then climb onto The Phoenix (1091 m), whose top is strewn with boulders. A sheltered saddle between The Phoenix and Centaurus Ridge has been used as an emergency camp.
legs.the-phoenix>west-portal-jn: Follow Centaurus Ridge south-east for about 3 km of undulating, partly overgrown ridge walking; the pad is faint and cairns are sparse, so navigation in cloud is serious. Federation Peak and the Eastern Arthurs fill the view to the east. Slopes then lead up the western ridge of West Portal to around the 1100 m contour, the usual pack-drop for the summit side trip. Skipping the summit saves about an hour.
legs.west-portal-jn>crags-of-andromeda: Follow the faint pad north along the crest of the Crags of Andromeda or just west of it, about an hour. High cliffs fall away on the east side, so keep well back in strong winds and poor visibility. This is very exposed, remote country with no easy escape.
legs.crags-of-andromeda>lake-rosanne: From the northern end of the Crags descend east into a valley. Contour to avoid the densest scrub; this is slow, scratchy going and easy to bash into dead ends. Grassier ground signals Lake Rosanne (633 m). Promontory to Rosanne is about 9.5–11 km and roughly 9 h with the West Portal summit (trailhiking).
legs.lake-rosanne>strike-creek-jn: Skirt the ridge south of Lake Rosanne, push through scrub at the outlet, then descend about 400 m down the moraine onto the flat, wet Strike Creek Plains. The pad is vague until you reach boardwalks near the junction with the Eastern Arthurs track; use the boot-wash point there. A quicker alternative described in older notes heads north-west across the plains from Rosanne, crossing two scrubby creeks (the second is Strike Creek, about 1.5 h), then holds the middle of the plains to meet McKays Track near Nine Mile Creek and Seven Mile Creek (a further 2.5 h). This bypasses Razorback and Cracroft but involves off-track navigation.
legs.strike-creek-jn>cracroft-jn: Cross Strike Creek, whose difficulty depends on recent rain, then head north-east over wet buttongrass to the low Razorback Ridge. Climb a couple of kilometres along it to the junction of the Huon and McKays tracks, just west of Cracroft Crossing. There are dry, flat sites at the forest edge, and water from the Cracroft River nearby. Do not plan to exit via the Huon Track: PWS currently reports it heavily blocked by fallen trees.
legs.cracroft-jn>seven-mile-creek: Follow McKays Track north-west around the north side of the Razorback, then west to cross its low crest, with good views back to the Western Arthurs. Descend the south side onto the Arthur Plains and continue north-west for about 5 km over muddy buttongrass, passing north of a wooded knoll. At Seven Mile Creek the Kappa Moraine route joins; it has good sheltered sites. Parts of McKays Track here are little used and confused by animal pads, so check your bearing.
legs.condominium-creek>high-camp-hut: Register and use the boot-cleaning station (phytophthora) at the car park. After a short flat start the track climbs the ridge relentlessly on steps and rough track, with few good rest spots. The climb is about 700 m by most accounts; PWS says around 900 m. Views over Lake Pedder and the Frankland Range open up as you gain height, but the upper slopes are exposed to wind. Carry water for the climb. PWS allows 2–3 h.
legs.high-camp-hut>mt-eliza: Fill up at the High Camp tank: PWS warns water is limited until Lonely Tarns. Above the hut the route scrambles up a steep dolerite boulder field to Mt Eliza (1289 m), roughly 240 m of ascent. The line is not always obvious; as a rule keep heading uphill. On the way down in cloud, take care not to drift off-line. Very exposed to wind; this is the point to turn back if conditions are poor.
legs.mt-eliza>mt-anne-jn: The track levels out across the Eliza Plateau heading north to a small saddle with tarns (seasonal water). After a slight rise it skirts the west side of Eve Peak across further boulder fields marked by cairns: about 500 m of boulder hopping that can take an hour. Map and compass skills are essential in mist (PWS). At the junction, straight on leads to the Mt Anne summit route and right leads to Shelf Camp.
legs.mt-anne-jn>shelf-camp: Turn right at the junction and walk a short distance down to Shelf Camp on its rock shelf facing Mt Anne. PWS gives 3.1 km and 2–3 h for High Camp to Shelf Camp. If you plan to climb Mt Anne, many parties set up camp first and do the summit as a light side trip from the junction.
legs.shelf-camp>the-notch: Water is scarce from here to Lonely Tarns (PWS), so fill up at the Shelf tarns. The route traverses the north side of the peaks with some scrambling and awkward downclimbs; it is not always obvious. Head across a boulder ridge and sidle around the left side of a rocky knoll, with Lots Wife in view, to arrive at the Notch, the gap before the main bulk of Mt Lot. Going clockwise, the descent into the Notch from the east side is generally straightforward.
legs.the-notch>mt-lot: The crux of the circuit is a climb of about 7 m out of the Notch. Bridge the crack to ledges on the right, step left onto a small triangular ledge and pull through on good holds at the top; a variant further right is more exposed. Most parties haul packs with a rope (PWS: carry about 15 m) and many protect less confident members with a line. Wet or icy rock makes it much harder, and there have been many rescues here, so turn back rather than force it. Beyond the Notch the route climbs around the base of Mt Lot's cliffs and scrambles to the summit area (1262 m); packs can be dropped for the summit.
legs.mt-lot>lonely-tarns: Descend Lightning Ridge, a sharp, rough dolerite spine with steep drops either side and some spots where packs need passing down. Near where the ridge flattens, before reaching Judds Charm (913 m), leave it and descend east through dense scrub, pandani and mossy roots to the moraine between Lake Picone and Judds Charm, then on to camp. Chapman warns about side pads towards the lake that branch off before the main track turns; check the map before following them. PWS allows 4.5–6.5 h for Shelf to Lonely Tarns, for only about 3 km.
legs.lonely-tarns>sarah-jane-jn: Follow the track around the large tarn in a horseshoe, then climb a small rise and head south. Expect a muddy plateau with boardwalk and rock slabs past several small tarns. The track passes east of Mt Sarah Jane, and a cairn marks the turnoff to its summit. Mist is common on this plateau and cairns can be hard to follow.
legs.sarah-jane-jn>anne-river-jn: A steep descent of nearly 600 m down the Mt Sarah Jane spur, overgrown in places, with slippery roots and poor visibility in tall scrub. It is reliably harder and slower than it looks on the map. At the bottom the track follows the Anne River through buttongrass to the Lake Judd junction; water is easy from the river and wetlands. Duckboards make progress quicker in the second half.
legs.anne-river-jn>red-tape-creek: From the Lake Judd junction, extensive planking and bridges protect the plains (PWS), though muddy holes remain. It is easy to get briefly turned around in the forest patches. Cross the Anne River on the suspension bridge and come out on Scotts Peak Road at the Red Tape Creek trailhead, where parking is on the west side of the road. PWS gives 12 km and 4.5–7 h for Lonely Tarns to Red Tape Creek.
legs.red-tape-creek>condominium-creek-r: About 8 km north along the gravel Scotts Peak Road back to the Condominium Creek car park. There is no public transport; most parties car-shuffle or walk while trying to hitch. The road is exposed and can be hot or wet, so carry water.

stops.scotts-peak: Huon Campground has about 10 forest sites, toilets, picnic shelter and untreated water. The BoM Scotts Peak rain gauge next to the campground is a handy check of recent rainfall before committing to the plains.
stops.junction-creek: Sheltered eucalypt forest with several open tent spots and a drop toilet; often busy. Check for overhanging limbs and fallen trees in high wind. The most sheltered site before Lake Oberon, so it is the default fall-back if the moraine is clagged in.
stops.moraine-a-foot: Stream with a small sandy beach: the last reliable water before the range. Sites are bare, overused ground, with no toilet.
stops.moraine-a-top: Treat this as the gateway to the range. If it is blowing a gale or in whiteout here, dropping back to the base or Junction Creek is far safer than pushing on to Cygnus.
stops.lake-cygnus: Sheltered on three sides by the ridge, exposed mainly to southerlies. Sources disagree on platform numbers (2 to 4); PWS-era notes give about 10 tents across platforms, a rubble area and beach sites. Fly-in toilet south of the platforms. Water from the lake or inflow streams; filter or treat.
stops.square-lake: The stream in the small forest patch before the lake is the most reliable water of the Cygnus–Oberon day.
stops.lake-oberon: Four platforms (two tents each, one cramped by a boulder), a sandy cove for about two more tents, and a toilet in the scrub before the platforms. Water from the outlet river or streams; filter. Crowded in season, so arrive early. Classic spot to turn back if Moraine A to here has been a struggle.
stops.mt-pegasus: Carry 15–20 m of light rope or cord for hauling, and expect to wait behind other parties at the hole.
stops.high-moor: Two platforms joined by boardwalk (about 9 tents) just below Mt Columba, with an open toilet. The stream beside the platforms is unreliable in dry spells. Very exposed to fronts; parties are regularly stormbound here, so carry spare food. Phone reception is sometimes possible on the upper moor. A low saddle east of camp is a fine sunrise spot over the Eastern Arthurs and Federation Peak.
stops.beggary-bumps: No water between High Moor and Haven Lake; start with full bottles.
stops.haven-lake: Four platforms (two tents each), with a drop toilet hidden in the scrub. The cirque is well sheltered, and the lake is the water source (filter). Haven is the natural base for the Mt Aldebaran side trip.
stops.lake-sirona: Fill up here: it is the last reliable water before the plains on the A–K. Camp only in calm weather, as it is fully open to the west.
stops.mt-scorpio: Last reliable mobile coverage; check the forecast here before choosing Kappa or the full traverse.
stops.kappa-moraine-top: Decision point. On the A–K, carry enough water for the 2–3 h descent to Seven Mile Creek; on the full traverse, Lake Vesta is about an hour away.
stops.seven-mile-creek: Sheltered regrowth sites for 4–5 tents; dig toilet holes at least 100 m from the creek. Treat the creek water.
stops.wullyawa-creek: Small clearing in shaded scrub for 2–3 tents, with a log crossing.
stops.junction-creek-r: Can flood in heavy rain; drier sites lie south of the creek, which is the side you arrive on from McKays Track.
stops.scotts-peak-r: Boot-wash station at the forest edge, then sign out at the registration booth.
stops.lake-vesta: A few sheltered sites on the north-east side, best treated as emergency or overflow camping.
stops.lake-juno: A small campsite near the outlet (halfwayanywhere) makes Juno a possible emergency stop.
stops.promontory-lake: Campsites are in the south-east corner, reached along the north and east shores. Poorly sheltered, so expect wind. Fill up for a long, waterless day to Rosanne.
stops.the-phoenix: The saddle between The Phoenix and Centaurus Ridge offers a sheltered emergency tent spot.
stops.west-portal-jn: West Portal (about 1191 m by trailhiking) is the highest point of the Western Arthurs, with views back along the whole range and across to the Eastern Arthurs.
stops.lake-rosanne: Sheltered sites behind the sandy beach; the lake is the water source.
stops.cracroft-jn: Dry, flat sites at the forest edge near Cracroft Crossing. Do not rely on the Huon Track as an exit: PWS currently reports it heavily blocked.
stops.condominium-creek: Small car park beside Scotts Peak Road with a boot-cleaning station. If car-shuffling, leave the second car at Red Tape Creek, about 8 km south.
stops.high-camp-hut: Memorial hut (High Camp, about 1030–1046 m) with a 5–6 person loft. It is grubby but welcome in bad weather. Toilet, rainwater tank, and tent sites about 150 m west. No fires on the circuit.
stops.mt-eliza: The 1289 m summit gives views over Lake Pedder, Edgar Bay and, on clear days, the Western Arthurs. The track crosses the top of the boulder field, so the summit cairn is barely a detour.
stops.mt-anne-jn: Cairned junction west of Eve Peak: straight on for Mt Anne, right for Shelf Camp.
stops.shelf-camp: Flat but rocky, uneven pads beside small tarns. A freestanding tent is near-essential; anchor it with rocks. Storms have flattened tents here. If full, there are sites a little east, or just north down the slope. Max stay 3 nights (PWS). Superb sunrise on Mt Anne.
stops.the-notch: No water. Check that someone in the party can rig a simple haul and belay before committing.
stops.mt-lot: Summit 1262 m (trailhiking/halfwayanywhere), with views of Lots Wife, Lake Judd and Lonely Tarns below.
stops.lonely-tarns: On the east side of the largest tarn, just a few metres from the water. Platforms have anchoring chains and there is a toilet pod; max stay 3 nights. A good base for a day trip to Lots Wife.
stops.sarah-jane-jn: The turnoff is marked by a cairn. Mist is common on this plateau.
stops.anne-river-jn: Water from the Anne River. Lake Judd has campsites near its outlet (no toilet) if you want to break the last day.
stops.red-tape-creek: Trailhead on Scotts Peak Road just over the Anne River suspension bridge, with parking on the west side.

sideTrips.name: Mt Hesperus (1098 m)
sideTrips.note: Leave packs on the moor where the track passes below the western face and scramble up boulders to the summit. Unmarked but short; good views back to Lake Pedder and along the range to come. Skip it in whiteout or strong westerlies; the moor is hard to navigate in cloud.

sideTrips.name: Lake Fortuna
sideTrips.note: From the saddle between Mt Hesperus and the Capella Crags, drop to the lake below and climb back (trailhiking/halfwayanywhere: 800 m return, about 40 min). A quiet glacial lake under the crags and a useful water stop on a dry day. The return climb is the effort; ascent figure is an estimate.

sideTrips.name: Mt Hayes summit (1119 m)
sideTrips.note: Unmarked scramble from where the track passes below the summit (about 40 min return per trailhiking and thehikinglife). Fine views along the range towards Procyon and Orion. Rocky and exposed; not worth it in mist.

sideTrips.name: Mt Orion / Mt Sirius (1151 m)
sideTrips.note: Two separate unmarked summits either side of the saddle, each about 800 m return. Sirius takes about 30 min return and Orion (1151 m) about 40–45 min; doing both takes about 1.6 km and 1.25 h. Rocky scrambles with big views down to Lake Oberon and across the Arthur Plains. Sirius sometimes has phone reception; leave packs at the saddle.

sideTrips.name: Mt Columba (1042 m)
sideTrips.note: A short climb from the saddle above High Moor, about 15 min return. A favourite sunset and sunrise spot, looking over the Beggary Bumps and east to Federation Peak.

sideTrips.name: Dorado Peak (1068 m)
sideTrips.note: About 1.2 km return but roughly 2 h, because of the scrambling and scrub (trailhiking/thehikinglife). Reached back towards the saddle below Capricorn, so it is often done as an afternoon trip from High Moor. Pools near Dorado can hold water in a wet season.

sideTrips.name: Mt Aldebaran (1107 m)
sideTrips.note: Leave the main track near the saddle above Haven Lake and follow a rough, cairned pad around rocky tors to the summit (2.2 km return, 2–3 h). Expect scrub and scrambling; the views over the eastern range and Promontory Lake are outstanding. Haven Lake makes the best base. Turn back in mist, which has defeated many attempts.

sideTrips.name: Mt Scorpio summit (1106 m)
sideTrips.note: A few minutes off the track, with an optional short scramble along a narrow summit ridge. It is the last peak of the A–K and gives a sweeping view back over the whole range. Trailhiking gives the height as 1108 m.

sideTrips.name: Carina Peak
sideTrips.note: Full traverse only. A scrubby scramble from near the Kappa/Vesta junction (trailhiking/halfwayanywhere: 1.4 km, about 1 h return). Views over Lakes Vesta and Juno and Promontory Lake. The ascent is an estimate.

sideTrips.name: West Portal summit (~1185 m)
sideTrips.note: Leave packs on the western ridge near the 1100 m contour and scramble up by the south side of the twin summits (0.8 km, 40–45 min return). It is the highest point of the Western Arthurs (trailhiking gives 1191 m), with views back over the whole traverse and across to the Eastern Arthurs and Federation Peak. Exposed; skip it in high wind or cloud.

sideTrips.name: Lake Venus
sideTrips.note: Listed by trailhiking and halfwayanywhere as a 600 m, 15 min return side trip on the Promontory to Rosanne stage. No route description was found, and the exact start point is unverified, so check it on the TASMAP 1:25k sheets before relying on it.

sideTrips.name: Mt Canopus
sideTrips.note: Listed by trailhiking and halfwayanywhere as 3.2 km and about 3 h return from the Promontory to Rosanne stage. Remote, off-track and scrubby. Only one solo trip report was found (turned back in icy rain), and the start point and ascent are unverified, so check the map.

sideTrips.name: Mt Anne summit (1423 m)
sideTrips.note: Go straight on at the junction, cross boulder fields through some muddy scrub, then follow a zig-zagging scramble with real fall potential. PWS calls it extremely exposed and says a safety line may be needed; route-finding near the top is tricky, with dead ends. Fatalities have occurred. Not in poor visibility, wind or wet. There is a summit logbook and 360-degree views over the South West. PWS lists 1413 m; most other sources say 1423 m.

sideTrips.name: Eve Peak (~1388 m)
sideTrips.note: The track skirts the west side of Eve Peak just before the junction, and a short unmarked boulder scramble reaches the top. It is a quieter alternative or addition to Mt Anne in marginal conditions, but still exposed. Figures are estimates; PWS gives 1388 m and one club report gives 1357 m.

sideTrips.name: Lots Wife
sideTrips.note: An off-track, scrubby day trip from Lonely Tarns or Lake Picone on taped and cairned pads that are easy to lose after treefalls (about 3–4 h return per bushwalk.com reports). Best done as a layover day with two nights at Lonely Tarns. The striking dolerite pinnacle gives close views of Mt Lot and Lightning Ridge. Distance and ascent are estimates.

sideTrips.name: Mt Sarah Jane
sideTrips.note: From the cairned turnoff, climb steep scree and unstable boulders to the summit (Wild magazine: about 1.2 km, 190 m, 1.5 h return). Cairns are sparse and hard to follow in mist, and loose blocks are a real hazard, so take care descending. Views over Lake Judd, the Anne massif and the impoundments.

sideTrips.name: Lake Judd
sideTrips.note: Follow the Lake Judd Track west from the Anne River junction through buttongrass and forest, 30–45 min each way (PWS: 2.2 km, 1.5 h return). A big glacial lake under the cliffs of Mt Sarah Jane and Schnells Ridge. Campsites near the outlet with no toilet. Muddy, with occasional boardwalk.
